resumen: Natural side light, an angle that fits the dish and speed: food that looks good enough to eat.

bloques.alt: Three drawings of a dish seen from different angles. 1, overhead: a round pizza seen from above, with its toppings spread out, for flat dishes. 2, at 45 degrees: a bowl seen in perspective, a good place to start. 3, side-on: a burger seen from the side, with the top bun, the patty and the bottom bun, for tall dishes.
bloques.pie: 1 Overhead: flat dishes. 2 At 45°: a good place to start. 3 Side-on: tall dishes.

bloques.texto: For food: soft natural light from the side, an angle that fits the height of the dish, and take the photo right away, before it changes.

The best light is soft, natural light, like from a big window, coming in from the side. Direct sun casts hard shadows: look for an overcast day. A white card or a sheet of paper next to the plate bounces light back into the shadows.

items: Overhead, for flat dishes, like a pizza or a table with several plates.
At about 45°, a good place to start: it works for many dishes.
Side-on, at the height of the plate, for tall ones, like a burger or a cake.
Food changes quickly (it melts, it dries out): take the photo soon.
A simple background and few objects around: let nothing compete with the plate.
In low light, use a tripod: it lets you lengthen the [[velocidad|shutter speed]].
Turn off the flash, especially on a phone or in a restaurant.
Indoor bulbs tint food orange: adjust the [[balance-de-blancos|white balance]].

bloques.texto: On many phones, tapping the screen on the plate focuses and lets you adjust the exposure (more in “Tap to focus and expose”). In a restaurant, look inside for the spot with the best light.
Put a plate next to a window, with the light coming in from the side, and photograph it from above, at 45° and side-on. Which one suits it best? Also try a white card next to the plate.
